$comment: Curated teaching briefs for 13 concepts that belong to products other than the Copilot Studio build experience: Microsoft Foundry, Agent Builder and declarative agents, the Microsoft 365 Copilot hub, SharePoint AI, and AI Builder. Every statement follows the Microsoft Learn pages listed in verifiedAgainst.

foundry-projects.definition: A Foundry project is the workspace where a team builds with models and agents, inside a larger Azure resource that holds shared settings.
foundry-projects.analogy: Think of it like a folder on a shared drive: the folder holds one team's work, and the drive sets the shared rules.

blocks.label: Azure resource
blocks.plain: Holds shared settings, such as network security and model deployments.

blocks.label: Project
blocks.plain: The workspace for one team or idea. It organizes agents, evaluations, and files.

blocks.label: Hub
blocks.plain: Classic portal only: a hub groups projects that share security settings and connections.

blocks.label: Access
blocks.plain: Roles that decide who on the team can use the project and its resources.

blocks.label: Two portals
blocks.plain: The new portal shows Foundry projects only. The classic portal shows every project type.

flow.label: Get ready
flow.plain: A person with an Azure subscription and a suitable role gets started.

flow.label: Pick a type
flow.plain: They pick a Foundry project, or a hub-based project if they need hub features.

flow.label: Create
flow.plain: The portal creates the project, and the resource or hub behind it if needed.

flow.label: Share
flow.plain: The team gets a role so they can use the project and its resources.

flow.label: Build
flow.plain: The team builds agents, tests models, and runs evaluations inside the project.

example.input: A Contoso team wants a safe place to try models and build its first agent.
example.output: A project the team can share. It holds their agents, evaluations, and files, and uses the settings of the resource it lives on.

whenToUse: You want one shared workspace for agents, models, and evaluations.
Several teams need their own space but the same security settings.
You want to give each team member the access they need.
whenNot: A hub-based project is only for features a Foundry project lacks.
New agents and model features are built for Foundry projects, not hub-based ones.
Custom names, security controls, or cost tags can need setup in the Azure portal.
foundry-projects.dataNote: Projects are units of isolation: agents in a project share its file storage, conversation history, and search indexes. You can bring your own Azure resources for control over sensitive data.
foundry-projects.needToKnow: Agents, evaluations, and files live in a project. Model deployments and security settings come from the resource or hub the project sits on. Knowing your project type tells you which portal and which features you can use.
foundry-projects.demo: Show the two portal versions side by side and point out which kinds of project each one lists.
foundry-projects.askTheRoom: Which of your teams could share one project, and which would need a project of their own?
foundry-projects.sayOutLoud: Think of a Foundry project as a team's workspace. Contoso's support team and sales team could each have a project, both using the security settings of one Azure resource.

quiz.q: What is a Foundry project?
options: A workspace for building with models and agents
quiz.why: A project organizes agents, evaluations, and files for a team. It sits on a larger Azure resource.

quiz.q: Which portal shows both hub-based projects and Foundry projects?
quiz.why: Only Foundry projects appear in the new portal. The classic portal shows every project type.

quiz.q: What do projects on the same Foundry resource usually share?
options: Settings such as network security and deployments
quiz.why: Each project can have its own access, but they share common settings from the parent resource.

model-deployment.definition: Deploying a model sets up a copy that apps can call, which you can try in a playground and limit with quota.
model-deployment.analogy: Think of it like a budget: your quota is the total you may use, and each deployment gets a share of it.

blocks.label: Model catalog
blocks.plain: A searchable list of more than 10,000 models from many providers.

blocks.label: Model card
blocks.plain: The details page for one model: facts, deployments, benchmarks, and license.

blocks.label: Deployment
blocks.plain: A copy of a model set up in your project for apps to call.

blocks.label: Playground
blocks.plain: A place to chat with a deployed model and compare up to three models.

blocks.label: Quota
blocks.plain: Your usage allowance per model and region, counted in tokens per minute.

flow.label: Browse
flow.plain: A person searches and filters the catalog and reads a model card.

flow.label: Decide
flow.plain: They weigh a model sold by Azure against one from partners and community.

flow.label: Deploy
flow.plain: They deploy the model, which gives it a name and a share of quota.

flow.label: Try it
flow.plain: They test prompts in a playground and can compare models side by side.

flow.label: Manage quota
flow.plain: They watch quota and free some up, or ask for more, when it runs low.

example.input: A Contoso developer wants to see how two models answer the same support question.
example.output: Both models are deployed, then compared side by side in the playground with the same prompt, so the developer can judge quality and speed.

whenToUse: You need to pick a model before building an app or agent.
You want to test prompts before you write production code.
You want to compare up to three models side by side.
whenNot: Shared quota is for temporary tests. Production needs its own quota.
Partner and community models get support from the companies that make them.
Some models exist only in some regions, so region can limit your choice.
model-deployment.dataNote: Models from other providers come with their own terms. Learn has separate data and privacy pages for models sold by Azure and for Claude models.
model-deployment.needToKnow: A model does nothing for your app until it is deployed. A deployment has a name that your code uses to reach it, and it takes a share of the quota for that model and region. When quota runs out, you free some or ask for more.
model-deployment.demo: Show a model card, then a deployed model answering one question in the playground, and its share of quota.
model-deployment.askTheRoom: What would you compare between two models before picking one: speed, quality, or cost?
model-deployment.sayOutLoud: Before Contoso builds a support agent, the team tries two models in the playground with the same question. They keep the one that answers best, and they check that they have enough quota to run it.

quiz.q: What does deploying a model give you?
options: A copy of the model that your apps can call
A new model trained from scratch
quiz.why: A deployment sets the model up in your project under a name your code can use.

quiz.q: What is a playground for?
options: Trying prompts and comparing models before you build
Training a model on your data
quiz.why: Playgrounds let you test models and agents without writing code first.

quiz.q: What is quota counted in?
quiz.why: Azure assigns quota per subscription, per region, and per model, in tokens per minute.

quiz.q: Who supports a model from the partners and community group?
quiz.why: Partner and community models are developed and supported by their providers.

choose-approach.definition: Choosing an approach means deciding whether you need a declarative agent at all, and which tool to build it with: Agent Builder, Copilot Studio, or code.

blocks.label: Declarative agent
blocks.plain: Defined by instructions, knowledge, and actions. Copilot's own orchestrator and model run it.

blocks.label: Agent Builder
blocks.plain: A guided tool inside Microsoft 365 Copilot for simple, quick agents.

blocks.label: Copilot Studio
blocks.plain: A separate app for workflows and connectors. Features vary by harness.

blocks.label: Code tools
blocks.plain: Developer tools, such as Agents Toolkit, for lower-level control.

flow.label: Need
flow.plain: A person describes the goal, the users, and where they will work.

flow.label: Reuse check
flow.plain: They check whether an approved agent already does the job.

flow.label: Match tool
flow.plain: They match needs to a tool: outside actions or channels point to Copilot Studio.

flow.label: Build
flow.plain: They build with that tool and record owners, knowledge, and dependencies.

flow.label: Grow
flow.plain: If needs grow, an Agent Builder agent can be copied to Copilot Studio.

example.input: Contoso wants an onboarding agent that answers from approved team content.
example.output: Agent Builder fits: instructions plus approved knowledge, shared inside the organization. If it later needs workflows or outside actions, copy it to Copilot Studio.

whenToUse: Instructions and supported knowledge meet the need: start with Agent Builder.
You need outside actions, workflow logic, or separate environments: look at Copilot Studio.
You need an outside channel, such as a customer website: look at Copilot Studio.
whenNot: Skip building a new agent if an approved one already fits.
Audience size alone is not a reason to leave Agent Builder.
Declarative agents keep Copilot's engine; for your own engine, use a custom engine agent.
choose-approach.dataNote: Agent Builder does not use the organization's Dataverse storage allowance. A copied agent is stored in Dataverse in the environment you pick.
choose-approach.needToKnow: A declarative agent runs on Copilot's own orchestrator and model, so you shape it with instructions, knowledge, and actions. That keeps it simple, but you do not control the engine. Needing more control, outside channels, or workflows is the signal to look at other tools.
choose-approach.demo: Show a one-page comparison of Agent Builder and Copilot Studio, then place the room's example agent on it.
choose-approach.askTheRoom: Think of an agent you want. Does it need outside actions or another channel, or only instructions and knowledge?
choose-approach.sayOutLoud: Fabrikam's HR team wants an onboarding helper. If it only needs instructions and approved documents, Agent Builder is enough. If it must update another system, they would look at Copilot Studio.

quiz.q: What runs a declarative agent?
quiz.why: Declarative agents use Copilot's orchestrator and models, so no extra hosting is needed.

quiz.q: Which need points toward Copilot Studio instead of Agent Builder?
options: Actions in an outside system, or a customer-facing channel
quiz.why: Agent Builder does not author actions for external services. Sharing across departments does not by itself need Copilot Studio.

quiz.q: What happens when you copy an Agent Builder agent to Copilot Studio?
options: The two agents stay in sync
quiz.why: Copying creates a snapshot, not a synchronized upgrade. Some knowledge and capabilities are not copied.

copilot-controls.definition: Copilot controls are the settings and tools that help a company decide who uses Copilot, what it can reach, and how it is run.

blocks.label: Security and governance
blocks.plain: Protects data that Copilot and agents create or use.

blocks.label: Management
blocks.plain: Covers licensing, agent lifecycle, and how Copilot is set up.

blocks.label: Measurement
blocks.plain: Shows adoption, productivity impact, and business value.

blocks.label: Everyday choices
blocks.plain: Choices such as web search, pinning, and who can use Copilot Chat.

flow.label: Use
flow.plain: Someone in the organization uses Copilot or an agent.

flow.label: Follow choices
flow.plain: Copilot follows the organization's choices, such as web search and pinning.

flow.label: Protect
flow.plain: Protections apply to the data Copilot and agents read or create.

flow.label: Report
flow.plain: Reports show how much people use Copilot and agents.

flow.label: Adjust
flow.plain: The organization reviews the results and adjusts its choices.

example.input: Contoso wants Copilot Chat available but wants a say in web search.
example.output: The organization decides whether Copilot may use the web. If it is allowed, each person can still choose to turn web content off.

whenToUse: You are rolling out Copilot and want clear choices about access.
You need to decide where Copilot appears for your people.
You want one plan for safety, management, and reports.
whenNot: What you see depends on licenses, features, and rollout, so it can differ.
Some choices live in another service, such as Microsoft Purview.
Some agent controls live in the Power Platform admin center.
copilot-controls.dataNote: When web search is on, Copilot sends Bing a short search query built from the prompt, not whole files. Prompts and responses stay in Microsoft 365 unless the customer directs otherwise.
copilot-controls.needToKnow: Copilot controls have three parts: security and governance, management, and measurement. Most choices are made in Microsoft admin tools, but some open other services, such as Microsoft Purview. Data protection, agent lifecycle, and billing topics all build on this framework.
copilot-controls.demo: Show a one-page map of the three parts and point to the admin area where each one lives.
copilot-controls.askTheRoom: If Copilot arrived tomorrow, what would worry you most: who can use it, what it can see, or what it costs?
copilot-controls.sayOutLoud: Before Contoso turns Copilot on for everyone, the IT team decides who gets it, whether it may search the web, and how they will measure use. Those choices are what we call Copilot controls.

quiz.q: What are the three parts of Copilot controls?
options: Security and governance, management, and measurement
quiz.why: Learn describes security and governance, management controls, and measurement and reporting.

quiz.q: If an organization allows web search, can a person still turn web content off for themselves?
quiz.why: A person can turn web content off. If the organization turns web search off, the person cannot turn it on.

quiz.q: Where might a Copilot choice be made?
options: Sometimes in another service, such as Microsoft Purview
quiz.why: Some Copilot settings link to other services where the change is made.

agent-lifecycle.definition: Agent lifecycle means following each agent from the day it is made to the day it is retired, with ways to block, delete, or reassign it.

blocks.label: Agent Registry
blocks.plain: The list of every agent the company can use, with owners and status.

blocks.label: Owner
blocks.plain: The person who maintains an agent. An agent can lose its owner.

blocks.label: Lifecycle actions
blocks.plain: Block or unblock, delete and restore, and assign a new owner.

blocks.label: Rules
blocks.plain: Rules that find agents meeting a condition and act on many at once.

blocks.label: Tags and feedback
blocks.plain: Labels to organize agents, and a choice about sharing feedback with developers.

flow.label: Created
flow.plain: People and teams create agents, and shared or published agents show up in the registry.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: An administrator reviews agents, owners, and status.

flow.label: Block
flow.plain: An unsafe or unwanted agent can be blocked for everyone.

flow.label: Delete
flow.plain: A deleted agent is kept for 30 days, then removed for good.

flow.label: Reassign
flow.plain: When an owner leaves, an administrator or a rule assigns a new one.

example.input: A Contoso employee who built an Agent Builder agent leaves the company.
example.output: The agent has no owner. An administrator can assign a new one. For Agent Builder agents, a rule can pass ownership to the former owner's manager.

whenToUse: An agent looks unsafe or out of policy and must stop quickly.
An agent lost its owner and needs someone responsible.
You manage many agents and want rules, not one-by-one work.
whenNot: Blocking an agent does not always remove its access to connected services.
Actions on one agent do not automatically cover the tools it uses.
Ownership can be reassigned only for Agent Builder and Copilot Studio agents.
agent-lifecycle.dataNote: A deleted agent is soft deleted: its details and related resources are kept for 30 days. It can be restored, or removed for good.
agent-lifecycle.needToKnow: Agents sit in a registry with owners, publishers, and status. Administrators act on one agent at a time, or on many with rules. Blocking changes who can use an agent, but it does not by itself change what the agent was allowed to reach.
agent-lifecycle.demo: Show an agent list with owners, then a block and a restore of a sample agent.
agent-lifecycle.askTheRoom: Who owns the agents your teams build today, and what happens to an agent when its owner leaves?
agent-lifecycle.sayOutLoud: At Contoso, people build agents all the time. IT needs to know who owns each one, to stop one that looks unsafe, and to bring back one that was deleted by mistake. That is agent lifecycle management.

quiz.q: How long can a deleted agent be restored?
quiz.why: A deleted agent is kept for 30 days. After that it is removed for good.

quiz.q: What does an agent management rule do?
options: Finds agents that match a condition and acts on many at once
quiz.why: Rules identify agents that meet conditions, let an administrator review them, and apply an action in bulk.

quiz.q: Does blocking an agent always remove its permissions to connected services?
quiz.why: Learn notes that blocking an agent does not necessarily revoke connected-service permissions.

copilot-data-protection.definition: Copilot data protection is a set of tools that find files shared too widely, limit what Copilot sees, and keep a log.
copilot-data-protection.analogy: Think of it like a building: some tools find doors left open, some keep visitors from wandering in, and some keep a visitor log.

blocks.label: Find oversharing
blocks.plain: Reports show sites that more people can reach than need to.

blocks.label: Limit discovery
blocks.plain: Keeps chosen sites out of Copilot answers and organization-wide search.

blocks.label: Block risky use
blocks.plain: Data loss prevention rules can stop Copilot from using sensitive prompts or labeled files.

blocks.label: Keep records
blocks.plain: Audit logs show who used Copilot and which files it touched.

blocks.label: Watch risk
blocks.plain: A dashboard shows data risks for Copilot and agents.

flow.label: Ask
flow.plain: A person asks Copilot a question.

flow.label: Permissions
flow.plain: Copilot works only with content that person is allowed to reach.

flow.label: Restrictions
flow.plain: Sites the organization has restricted stay out of its answers.

flow.label: Rules
flow.plain: A data loss prevention rule can stop sensitive prompts or labeled files.

flow.label: Record
flow.plain: The interaction is written to the audit log.

flow.label: Watch
flow.plain: Dashboards flag data risk so the organization can act.

example.input: A Contoso employee asks Copilot about a payroll site that too many people can open.
example.output: Reports can flag that site as overshared. Restricting discovery keeps it out of Copilot answers while owners fix access.

whenToUse: You are preparing to roll out Copilot and agents.
You suspect files are shared more widely than needed.
You must show auditors what Copilot did.
whenNot: These tools do not fix permissions by themselves; access still needs review.
Some tools need extra licenses or admin roles, so check what applies.
Use restricted discovery sparingly. Too much of it hides useful content from Copilot.
copilot-data-protection.dataNote: These tools change what Copilot can find or use, not who has permission. Restricted discovery leaves permissions and the search index unchanged.
copilot-data-protection.needToKnow: Copilot works with what a person can already reach, so oversharing becomes a Copilot problem. Reports find it. Restricted discovery limits it while you fix it. Data loss prevention blocks sensitive use. Audit logs and dashboards show what happened.
copilot-data-protection.demo: Show a sample oversharing report, then a sample audit record for one Copilot use.
copilot-data-protection.askTheRoom: If Copilot could read everything you can open today, what would surprise you?
copilot-data-protection.sayOutLoud: Copilot works with what each person can already open. So before Contoso turns it on, the team looks for files and sites that are shared too widely, and sets up a record of how Copilot is used.

quiz.q: Why does oversharing matter for Copilot?
options: Copilot can use content a person can reach, even if it was shared too widely
quiz.why: Copilot access is scoped by user permissions, so content that is open to many people can show up for them.

quiz.q: What does Restricted Content Discovery change?
options: Whether a site's content shows up in organization-wide search and Copilot
Who has permission to the site
quiz.why: It affects discovery, not permissions. People who already have access can still open the content.

quiz.q: Which tool records Copilot interactions?
quiz.why: Audit records note who used Copilot, when, where, and which files or sites it used.

copilot-metering.definition: Pay-as-you-go billing charges for Copilot services by how much they are used, not by a license for each person.
copilot-metering.analogy: Think of it like a utility bill: you pay for what you use, and a budget sends alerts as you near your limit.

blocks.label: Billing policy
blocks.plain: Links a group of users to an Azure subscription that pays for their use.

blocks.label: Connection
blocks.plain: Joins the policy to a Copilot service, such as Copilot Chat or SharePoint agents.

blocks.label: Budget
blocks.plain: An optional limit that sends email alerts. It does not stop usage.

blocks.label: Meter
blocks.plain: Azure measures usage and charges it to the subscription.

blocks.label: Cost reports
blocks.plain: Reports show costs and usage for each service.

flow.label: Create policy
flow.plain: An admin creates a billing policy linked to an Azure subscription.

flow.label: Add people
flow.plain: They add the users or groups the policy covers.

flow.label: Connect
flow.plain: They connect the policy to a Copilot service.

flow.label: Use
flow.plain: People in the group use the service, and their use is metered.

flow.label: Watch cost
flow.plain: Cost reports and budget alerts show how spending is going.

example.input: Contoso wants to try Copilot Chat agents with a few teams before buying licenses.
example.output: A billing policy covers those teams. They use the agents, Contoso pays only for use, and the usage shows how much people adopt them.

whenToUse: You want to try Copilot services before buying licenses.
Usage will rise and fall, so a fixed fee does not fit.
You want costs assigned to a department.
whenNot: A budget only sends alerts; spending can go past it.
Creating a policy is not enough; it must be connected to a service.
Pay-as-you-go is off by default.
copilot-metering.needToKnow: Billing happens in two steps: create a billing policy, then connect it to a service. The policy links users to an Azure subscription. A budget warns but does not stop use, and disconnecting the policy ends access for its users.
copilot-metering.demo: Show a sample billing policy with its subscription, budget, and connected service.
copilot-metering.askTheRoom: Which of your teams would try Copilot only if they could pay for what they actually use?
copilot-metering.sayOutLoud: Contoso is not sure every team needs a license. So it sets up pay-as-you-go: one billing policy, one Azure subscription, and a budget that warns when spending gets high.

quiz.q: What does a billing policy link together?
quiz.why: A billing policy ties a set of users to the Azure subscription that is billed for their use.

quiz.q: What does a budget do?
options: Sends email alerts as spending grows
Stops all use at the limit
quiz.why: The system does not enforce the budget. Usage can continue after it is passed.

quiz.q: After creating a billing policy, what else is needed?
options: Connect it to a Copilot service
quiz.why: Creating a policy does not finish setup. It must be connected to the service.

ai-capability-selection.definition: Choosing an AI capability means matching a business problem to the AI Builder model or prompt that fits, before you build.

blocks.label: Data type
blocks.plain: What the AI works on: documents, text, structured data, or images.

blocks.label: Prebuilt model
blocks.plain: Ready to use with no training, for jobs common to many businesses.

blocks.label: Custom model
blocks.plain: Trained on your own data, for needs unique to your business.

blocks.label: Prompt
blocks.plain: Instructions to a generative AI model, such as a request to summarize text.

blocks.label: Region
blocks.plain: Where your environment runs decides which models are available.

flow.label: Start
flow.plain: A maker starts with the business problem, such as expense reports.

flow.label: Data type
flow.plain: They find the data type: documents, text, structured data, or images.

flow.label: Prebuilt or custom
flow.plain: They decide between a ready-made model and a custom model.

flow.label: Check region
flow.plain: They check that the model is available in their region.

flow.label: Build
flow.plain: Then they try the model or build it.

example.input: Contoso wants to sort customer feedback by how positive it sounds.
example.output: A prebuilt sentiment model fits. For Contoso's own topics, a custom model that sorts text fits better.

whenToUse: You are not sure which AI Builder model fits your problem.
You want a prebuilt model when the job is common to many businesses.
You need to check whether a model is available in your region.
whenNot: Prebuilt models may not fit data unique to your business; consider custom.
Some features are in preview; check release status before relying on them.
ai-capability-selection.dataNote: AI Builder models run in the region that hosts your Power Platform environment, so what is available follows that region.
ai-capability-selection.needToKnow: AI Builder offers prebuilt models that work right away and custom models you train on your data. Each model works on one kind of data. Availability and release status depend on the region of your environment.
ai-capability-selection.demo: Show the list of model types grouped by data type, then pick one for a sample business problem.
ai-capability-selection.askTheRoom: Name one repetitive task in your team that involves reading text or documents. Which model type might help?
ai-capability-selection.sayOutLoud: Contoso gets hundreds of expense receipts a week. A prebuilt model reads receipts, so nobody has to train anything. A different problem, like predicting late shipments, needs a custom model trained on Contoso's own history.

quiz.q: What is a prebuilt model?
options: A model that is ready to use, with no training
A model you train on your own data
A model that only works offline
quiz.why: Prebuilt models let you go straight to using AI for common business scenarios.

quiz.q: Which model type fits predicting whether an account will pay its invoices on time?
quiz.why: Prediction models learn from historical data that you provide and predict outcomes such as yes or no.

quiz.q: Why does the region of your environment matter?
options: Models are deployed there, and release status varies by region
It decides the color of the app
quiz.why: Your AI Builder models run in the region that hosts your environment, and each region has its own availability.

learn.title: AI models and business scenarios
Overview of AI Builder
Feature availability by region

prebuilt-ai-models.definition: A prebuilt model is an AI Builder model that is ready to use, with no training, for common jobs such as reading receipts.

blocks.label: Input
blocks.plain: Text, or a file such as a receipt, that you give the model.

blocks.label: Model
blocks.plain: A ready-made model, such as one that reads receipts.

blocks.label: Output
blocks.plain: Labels, scores, or fields, often with a confidence value.

blocks.label: Flow or app
blocks.plain: Where the model is called and its result is used.

flow.label: Send
flow.plain: A person, a flow, or an app gives the model text or a file.

flow.label: Read
flow.plain: The model reads it. No training is needed.

flow.label: Return
flow.plain: It returns results, such as a sentiment label or receipt fields.

flow.label: Confidence
flow.plain: Confidence scores show how sure the model is.

flow.label: Use
flow.plain: The flow or app uses the results in later steps.

example.input: A Contoso customer review: 'The delivery was late, but support was great.'
example.output: An overall label, such as mixed, plus a label and a confidence score for each sentence.

whenToUse: The job is common across many businesses, such as receipts or reviews.
You want results without collecting training data.
You want to try a model before building a flow.
whenNot: Your data is unique to your business; a custom model may fit better.
Models have limits, such as file size or text length, so check them first.
Some prebuilt models are in preview; check release status.
prebuilt-ai-models.needToKnow: Prebuilt models work out of the box, but each has rules about the language, file type, and size it accepts. They return results with confidence scores that show how sure the model is.
prebuilt-ai-models.demo: Show the sentiment model scoring a short sample review, with its label and confidence scores.
prebuilt-ai-models.askTheRoom: Where do your people read piles of text or paper, such as reviews or receipts, that a model could sort?
prebuilt-ai-models.sayOutLoud: Contoso gets customer reviews every day. A prebuilt sentiment model can mark each one as positive, negative, neutral, or mixed, without anyone training it first.

quiz.q: What makes a model prebuilt?
options: It is trained on your data
quiz.why: Prebuilt models are ready for common business scenarios right away.

quiz.q: What does a confidence score show?
options: How sure the model is about a result
quiz.why: Scores run from 0 to 1. Values close to 1 mean greater confidence.

quiz.q: Which of these is a prebuilt model?
quiz.why: Receipt processing is prebuilt. Prediction and object detection are custom models you train.

learn.title: Sentiment analysis prebuilt model
Receipt processing prebuilt model
AI models and business scenarios

ai-consumption.definition: Using AI in apps and flows means calling a prompt or model from a flow or canvas app, then using its result in later steps.

blocks.label: Prompt or model
blocks.plain: The AI piece you built or picked, ready to be called.

blocks.label: Flow action
blocks.plain: A flow step that runs a prompt or model and passes on the result.

blocks.label: App formula
blocks.plain: In a canvas app, a Power Fx formula calls the model.

blocks.label: Output
blocks.plain: The text, label, or fields that later steps use.

blocks.label: Access
blocks.plain: People need access to the model, flow, or app to run it.

flow.label: Start
flow.plain: Something starts the flow, such as a button or a new file.

flow.label: Send input
flow.plain: The flow or app sends input to the prompt or model.

flow.label: Get result
flow.plain: The AI returns text, labels, or fields.

flow.label: Review
flow.plain: Optionally, a person reviews the result before it is used.

flow.label: Use it
flow.plain: The flow or app uses the result, such as posting a message.

example.input: A Contoso team wants a short summary of each support email posted to a chat.
example.output: A flow sends the email text to a saved prompt and posts the generated summary to a chat.

whenToUse: You already have flows or apps and want to add AI to them.
You want a person to approve generated text before it is used.
You want one saved prompt reused in more than one place.
whenNot: AI output can be wrong; keep a person in the loop for important text.
Prompts run only in some regions and can be limited by capacity.
ai-consumption.needToKnow: A model or prompt is only useful once something calls it. Flows use an action for each model. Canvas apps call models with Power Fx formulas. People also need permission to use the model, and a model must be shared before others can run it.
ai-consumption.demo: Show a flow that sends sample text to a prompt and posts the answer to a chat.
ai-consumption.askTheRoom: Which flow or app you already use would be better with one AI step added?
ai-consumption.sayOutLoud: Contoso already has a flow that handles new support emails. Adding one prompt step to summarize each email puts AI into work people already do.

quiz.q: How does a canvas app call an AI Builder model?
quiz.why: Power Fx expressions let a canvas app use AI Builder models.

quiz.q: Why add a person to review AI text in a flow?
options: To check quality and make sure it meets standards
To make the flow run faster
quiz.why: Human review helps make sure generated output is high quality and meets requirements.

quiz.q: By default, who can use a model you create?
options: Only you, until it is shared
quiz.why: A model or prompt is only available to its owner until it is shared.

learn.title: Use your prompt in Power Automate
AI Builder in Power Apps overview
AI Builder in Power Automate overview

content-ai.definition: Content AI reads documents and files and pulls out structured details, such as dates, names, and totals, so they can be saved and searched.

blocks.label: Document
blocks.plain: The input: a file in a library, or a document sent to a model.

blocks.label: Model or prompt
blocks.plain: A prebuilt or custom model, or a plain-language prompt.

blocks.label: Fields
blocks.plain: Where the extracted details are saved, such as library columns.

blocks.label: Review
blocks.plain: A person checks results, because AI output can be wrong.

flow.label: Add file
flow.plain: A file is added to a library, or sent into a flow.

flow.label: Read
flow.plain: The AI reads the content of the file.

flow.label: Extract
flow.plain: It finds the details it was asked for, using a model or a prompt.

flow.label: Save
flow.plain: It saves the results as columns or fields.

flow.label: Use
flow.plain: People or flows use them for search, sorting, or the next step.

example.input: Contoso receives hundreds of vendor contracts as files in a SharePoint library.
example.output: AI can fill in columns like the party name and end date from each contract. People can then search and sort instead of reading every file.

whenToUse: You have many files with the same kinds of details inside.
You want details in columns so you can search and filter.
A prebuilt model already matches your document type.
whenNot: AI-generated content might be wrong, so check the results.
Some file types, library types, and column types are not supported.
Layouts that prebuilt models miss may need a custom model.
content-ai.dataNote: Autofill reads the text of a file and saves the answer to a column. Encrypted files are not analyzed.
content-ai.needToKnow: Content AI comes in three forms. Prebuilt models handle common documents such as invoices and contracts. Custom models learn your own layouts from examples. Autofill uses a plain-language prompt. All of them save what they find so it can be searched and reused.
content-ai.demo: Show a library where autofill columns have filled in details from a few sample files.
content-ai.askTheRoom: Which documents does your team read again and again just to copy details into a list?
content-ai.sayOutLoud: Think of a stack of Contoso invoices. Instead of someone typing each due date and amount into a list, an AI model reads each invoice and fills in those fields. A person then checks the results.

quiz.q: What does content AI produce from a document?
options: Structured details such as dates and totals
quiz.why: It extracts or generates details and saves them, for example to library columns.

quiz.q: What does an autofill column use to decide what to extract?
options: A model trained on five documents
quiz.why: Autofill columns use natural language prompts. Trained document models are a different option.

quiz.q: Why should people check the results?
quiz.why: Learn reminds readers to check autofill results because generated content can be wrong.

learn.title: Overview of autofill columns
Overview of document processing model types
Document processing model overview

custom-ai-models.definition: A custom model is an AI Builder model you train on your own data, then check, improve, and publish so people can use it.

blocks.label: Training data
blocks.plain: Your own examples, such as tagged text or past outcomes, kept in Dataverse.

blocks.label: Training
blocks.plain: An automatic step that teaches the model from your data.

blocks.label: Performance score
blocks.plain: A score on the details page that helps you compare versions.

blocks.label: Version
blocks.plain: You can hold a published version and a last trained version.

blocks.label: Publish
blocks.plain: Lets everyone in the environment use that version.

flow.label: Set up
flow.plain: A maker picks a model type and points it at their data.

flow.label: Train
flow.plain: AI Builder trains the model.

flow.label: Evaluate
flow.plain: The maker reviews performance and can test it on real examples.

flow.label: Improve
flow.plain: If it falls short, they create a new version or retrain on fresh data.

flow.label: Publish
flow.plain: They publish the version they want people to run.

flow.label: Use
flow.plain: Flows and apps call the published model.

example.input: Contoso has years of support tickets tagged by topic.
example.output: A category classification model learns from those tags. Once published, it sorts new tickets into the same topics.

whenToUse: Your data or categories are unique to your business.
You have past examples with known tags or outcomes.
You want to predict a result from historical records.
whenNot: A prebuilt model may already do the job without training.
A model is only as good as its data; poor data gives poor results.
Only two trained versions are kept: one published and one last trained.
custom-ai-models.dataNote: Training data and model settings are stored in Dataverse. A model belongs to its owner until it is shared, and its training files can be seen only by its creator and administrators.
custom-ai-models.needToKnow: Training builds a version of the model. You can hold two versions: the published one and the last trained one. Training with new settings creates a new version, and retraining reuses the same settings on new data. Publishing makes a version available.
custom-ai-models.demo: Show a trained model's details page with its performance score, a published version, and a newer trained version.
custom-ai-models.askTheRoom: What past outcomes or tagged records does your team already keep that a model could learn from?
custom-ai-models.sayOutLoud: Contoso has years of orders and knows which ones arrived late. A custom prediction model can learn from that history and flag new orders likely to be late. Before anyone relies on it, the team checks its score and publishes the version they trust.

quiz.q: What does training do?
options: Teaches the model from your data
quiz.why: Training is an automatic process that teaches the model to solve your business problem.

quiz.q: What is retraining?
options: A new version that uses the same settings on new data
quiz.why: Retraining studies new data so the model stays accurate over time.

quiz.q: A prediction model scores near perfect in training but fails on new records. What is a likely cause?
options: A column gives away the answer
The model has too few users
quiz.why: A column that only exists after the outcome, such as a delivered date, makes the model look better than it is.
